checks_run.procedure: Judge the two open questions of D-238: D-229 (connector configuration names stay cannot-name) and D-228 (4) (cross-organization ids are out of scope). Read the connector permissions (packages/shared/src/permissions.ts), checkFieldMappings, ADR-0051 part E/F, and every caller of maskHiddenIds, hiddenIdsInTexts and maskRestrictedIdsInFields. Run the reference-inventory, version-bound token (z15) and served-error-text (z13c) suites.
checks_run.command: grep connector.read packages/shared/src/permissions.ts; grep -rn maskHiddenIds apps/api/src; vitest (DOM-RG1-04)
checks_run.expected: Either no served column, response, channel or write path names a sensitive record to a reader who cannot read it, or a finding.
checks_run.actual: Not a defect. Wording note: D-229 says connector configuration is seen by 'connector administrators'. In fact connector.read, and with it fieldMappings and credentialRefs, is held by TO, KDS, TD, AUD and ADM_TECH. A mapping is a free-text {source, target}. target must match ^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9_]{0,63}$; source is free text of 1 to 100 characters, and only configurers (ADM_TECH) write it. So the only way a mapping can 'name' a sensitive id is for a configurer to type one. That is the same class as any human free text (descriptions, notes), which no module masks. D-223 already accepts it, and UUIDv7 ids are not guessable. Masking applies where the product itself writes an id into a key or an error text: integrations routes, automation executions and failures, exceptions and corrective cases. The run's error text that repeats a mapping is masked. credential_refs hold only SecretRef provider and name, set through IT's manifest. I found no response or channel where the product discloses a hidden id. The z13c, z13b and z15 suites, the inventory (open 0) and the version-bound token suites pass, so my token-sequence attempts (edits, grant changes and concurrent saves, as those suites drive them) lost no literal. D-228 (4): every helper checks the reader's own organizations, and a reader never reaches another organization's record. The fault path that remains needs an envelope naming another organization's record. I accept both, with the wording note above for D-229.

checks_run.procedure: Judge D-203, D-204 and D-205 against the master prompt's automation clauses (REQ-S12-019, REQ-S20-013). Read ADR-0043's amendments E1-E2 and G1-G4 and the worker engine's action-key composition, and run the automation suites (automation-version-at-occurrence, automation-backlog-enablement, automation-engine and others).
checks_run.expected: Late events are evaluated against the version enabled at their occurrence. Disabling a rule stops pending events. The residual race does not duplicate approvals, measurements or notifications.
checks_run.actual: Accepted. D-203 (no action on events from before enablement) follows the principle that a record keeps the configuration version in force when it was made. D-204 (the version at occurrence, from the append-only enablement ledger 0122/0123) means a backlog at publish no longer drops automations silently. D-205's kill switch gives administrators operational control. Residual race (G4): it needs a rule transaction that overlaps the event's relay-and-evaluate cycle and a second evaluation of the same envelope. The worst case is a second execution by another version, because the execution UNIQUE is per version. But the action idempotency key is automationActionKey({ruleCode, triggerKey, ordinal}), with no version in it, so an action completed at the same ordinal returns 'already'. Duplication is bounded to an action at a different ordinal in the other version, inside a window the ADR documents honestly. Automations never decide business approvals (shown on the Operations page). The race is acceptable as documented. Every automation suite passes.
